props.gloss_en: the mishna: the Sages stated a GREAT principle with regard to Shabbat
proposed: he says 'a great principle' because he goes on to teach 'they stated another principle'; and so with Shevi'it
R' Yosei bar Avin: Shabbat and Shevi'it, which have primary categories and derivatives, he called 'great'; tithes, which have none, he did not
rather, this is the reason: the punishment of Shabbat is greater than that of Shevi'it, and the punishment of Shevi'it greater than that of tithes
the tithes mishna teaches 'they stated another principle' and does not open with 'a great principle'
bar Kappara's text of the tithes mishna reads 'a great principle'
the punishment of Shabbat is greater than that of Shevi'it
Shabbat applies both to what is detached and to what is attached [to the ground]
Shevi'it does not apply to what is detached; it applies to what is attached
the punishment of Shevi'it is greater than that of tithes
Shevi'it applies both to human food and to animal food
tithes apply to human food; they do not apply to animal food
for bar Kappara, who teaches 'a great principle' for tithes: the punishment of tithes is greater than that of pe'a
tithes apply to figs and vegetables
pe'a does not apply to figs and vegetables
the mishna (Pe'a 1:4): they stated a principle for pe'a -- whatever is food, guarded, grows from the ground, is gathered at once and brought in for storage is obligated in pe'a
'food' excludes the aftergrowths of satis and madder
'guarded' excludes ownerless produce
'grows from the ground' excludes truffles and mushrooms
'gathered at once' excludes the fig
'brought in for storage' excludes vegetables
the mishna (Ma'asrot 1:1): they stated a principle for tithes -- whatever is food, guarded and grows from the ground is obligated in tithes
